title: Dharmapala
hookLine: the Sri Lankan layman who campaigned to restore Bodh Gaya and spoke in Chicago

lines: A YOUNG MAN IN WHITE AT BODH GAYA.
HE DECIDES TO USE HIS VOICE.
cards: A young man from Colombo, dressed in white, comes to Bodh Gaya on pilgrimage. He has read about this place: the tree, the seat of awakening.
What he finds is a temple in poor repair, in the hands of others, with few Buddhists to be seen.
By his own account, he sits near the tree and makes up his mind: he will give his life to bringing Buddhists back to this place. He has no title. He isn't a monk.
He isn't a king. What he has is a voice, and he decides to use it.

teach.h: ANAGARIKA: A LAYMAN WHO LEFT HOME.
teach.b: First, the name and the white cloth. He was born into a Sri Lankan family and took the name Dharmapala, protector of the Dharma, along with the title Anagarika, one who has left home.
He lived without marrying and gave himself to the teaching, but through his campaigning years he stayed a layman; he was ordained a monk only near the end of his life.
Second, Bodh Gaya. The temple and its lands had long been held by a Hindu monastery, under its head, the mahant. Dharmapala wanted Buddhists to have a say at the place of awakening.

He founded a society to work for it, wrote, petitioned, raised money, and went to court. He did not win in his lifetime. After his death, the law set up a committee of Hindus and Buddhists to care for the temple together.
Both sides held the place dear, and the answer, in the end, was to share it.
Third, Chicago. At a great gathering of the world's religions held there, he stood up and spoke for Buddhism to an American audience. Fourth, the whole man.
Some of his writing was hard, even harsh, toward other communities, and historians still argue over that part of his legacy.
He's remembered with admiration and with argument, both. But the thread through all of it is clear: he loved something, and he wouldn't keep quiet about it.

how: Dharmapala is remembered in Sri Lanka and India as a Buddhist reformer, and the society he founded still works for Buddhist sites and pilgrims, while the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is cared for by a committee of Hindus and Buddhists.

games.q: you're a young Sri Lankan layman at Bodh Gaya, and the temple you've dreamed of is in poor repair, in other hands. you have no title and no office. what do you do?
o: go home sad and say nothing.
decide to give your life to speaking up for it.
take holy orders and stay as a monk at the temple.
games.why: by his own account, he resolved there to give his life to it, and he spent it writing, petitioning, and speaking as a layman; he was ordained a monk only near the end of his life.

practice: Choose one thing you care about that could use a voice, a place, a person, a practice, and find one honest, kind sentence you could say for it.
Say it silently a few times, and if it carries any heat or harshness, soften it until it's a sentence you'd be glad to hear said about something you love.
